title: Artificial Intelligence: Principles and Techniques
one: The overview course for AI: search, MDPs, graphical models, logic, and machine learning under one frame — making good decisions with incomplete information and limited compute.
pos: CS 221 is the entry point to Stanford's AI track, and the best way to see that AI is more than model tuning. It uses one mathematical language (probability + algorithms) to describe how agents make decisions with incomplete information and limited computation, spanning classical symbolic AI through modern machine learning.
topics: **Search and constraint satisfaction**: DFS/BFS/A*, heuristics, CSPs, local search
**Games and adversarial search**: minimax, alpha-beta, expected utility
**MDPs and reinforcement learning**: value iteration, policy iteration, Q-learning basics
**Probabilistic graphical models**: Bayesian networks, HMMs, variable elimination, sampling
**Machine learning**: naive Bayes, perceptron, logistic regression, losses and regularization
**Logic and knowledge representation**: propositional logic, first-order logic, inference
**Capstone project**: combine the modules into a working AI system
prereq: CS 103 (or 103B/X), CS 106B (or 106X), CS 109, and CS 161. The course explicitly says it will not reteach these foundations.
assessment: Typically about five written/programming assignments plus a midterm, a final, and a capstone project; the workload is on the heavy side for a Stanford course. Check the current syllabus for exact weights.
who: Undergrads or students switching majors who want a complete AI map; anyone planning to take CS 229/224N/234 next; engineers who want to fill the classical-AI gap.
tips: Brush up on probability (CS 109) and algorithms (CS 161) first, or the assignments will hurt. Write the search and MDP parts from scratch rather than only calling libraries.
description: Artificial intelligence (AI) has had a huge impact in many areas, including medical diagnosis, speech recognition, robotics, web search, advertising, and scheduling. This course focuses on the foundational concepts that drive these applications. In short, AI is the mathematics of making good decisions given incomplete information (hence the need for probability) and limited computation (hence the need for algorithms). Specific topics include search, constraint satisfaction, game playing,n Markov decision processes, graphical models, machine learning, and logic. Prerequisites: CS 103 or CS 103B/X, CS 106B or CS 106X, CS 109, and CS 161 (algorithms, probability, and object-oriented programming in Python). We highly recommend comfort with these concepts before taking the course, as we will be building on them with little review.

title: Machine Learning (STATS 229)
one: Stanford's flagship ML course: a single probabilistic and statistical frame that connects supervised learning, unsupervised learning, and learning theory.
pos: CS 229 is one of Stanford's most classic and influential machine-learning courses, and it goes noticeably deeper than CS 230. It is less about how to call a model and more about the assumptions, losses, optimization, and generalization behind it — the foundation for research or a PhD.
topics: **Supervised learning**: linear/logistic regression, GLMs, SVMs, kernels, trees and ensembles
**Learning theory**: bias-variance, regularization, feature selection, generalization and model selection
**Unsupervised learning**: k-means, GMMs, EM, PCA, ICA, density estimation
**Deep learning basics**: neural networks, backpropagation, training techniques
**Reinforcement learning**: MDPs, value iteration, policy search, adaptive control
**Course project**: usually an open-ended ML research or application project
prereq: Python/NumPy programming (CS 106A/B level); probability (CS 109/MATH 151/STATS 116); multivariable calculus and linear algebra (MATH 51/CS 205).
assessment: Typically 4–5 problem sets plus a midterm and a final project; about 10–15 hours per week. Check the current syllabus for exact weights.
who: People who want to understand the math behind ML and later do research or a PhD; engineers who already use scikit-learn but want the derivations and theory; interview candidates who want more than memorized answers.
tips: Write the problem-set derivations yourself, especially GLMs, the SVM dual, and EM. Pair it with CS 229M or STATS 315A to fill in the theory side.
description: Topics: statistical pattern recognition, linear and non-linear regression, non-parametric methods, exponential family, GLMs, support vector machines, kernel methods, deep learning, model/feature selection, learning theory, ML advice, clustering, density estimation, EM, dimensionality reduction, ICA, PCA, reinforcement learning and adaptive control, Markov decision processes, approximate dynamic programming, and policy search. Prerequisites: knowledge of basic computer science principles and skills at a level sufficient to write a reasonably non-trivial computer program in Python/NumPy to the equivalency of CS106A, CS106B, or CS106X, familiarity with probability theory to the equivalency of CS 109, MATH151, or STATS 116, and familiarity with multivariable calculus and linear algebra to the equivalency of MATH51 or CS205.
instructors: Re, C.; Ma, T.; Fox, E.

title: Deep Learning
one: Ng's hands-on deep learning course: from fully connected networks to CNNs/RNNs, focused on making DL projects succeed, not just deriving formulas.
pos: CS 230 uses a flipped classroom: watch videos and do programming assignments and quizzes before class, then discuss and work on projects in class. It covers the building blocks and engineering methodology of deep learning, with case studies across healthcare, autonomous driving, sign language, music generation, and NLP. It is more hands-on than CS 229.
topics: **Neural network basics**: forward/backward propagation, activations, losses
**CNNs**: convolution, pooling, classic architectures, transfer learning
**Training techniques**: Adam, dropout, BatchNorm, Xavier/He initialization
**ML project methodology**: error analysis, bias-variance, data splits, iteration strategy
**Industry case studies**: medical imaging, autonomous driving, music generation, NLP
prereq: Python programming; linear algebra (matrix/vector operations). CS 229 may be taken concurrently.
assessment: Programming assignments, online quizzes, and an open-ended final project; the flipped classroom requires preparation before class. Check the current syllabus for details.
who: People who want to get hands-on with deep learning and ship a complete project; product or startup backgrounds that need technical execution; a broader, project-oriented route than CS 231N.
tips: If you have never touched DL, start with the NN part of CS 229 or the first few CS 231N lectures. The project separates people more than the assignments do — form a team and pick a topic early.
description: Deep Learning is one of the most highly sought after skills in AI. We will help you become good at Deep Learning. In this course, you will learn the foundations of Deep Learning, understand how to build neural networks, and learn how to lead successful machine learning projects. You will learn about Convolutional networks, RNNs, LSTM, Adam, Dropout, BatchNorm, Xavier/He initialization, and more. You will work on case studies from healthcare, autonomous driving, sign language reading, music generation, and natural language processing. You will master not only the theory, but also see how it is applied in industry. You will practice all these ideas in Python and in TensorFlow, which we will teach. AI is transforming multiple industries. After this course, you will likely find creative ways to apply it to your work. This class is taught in the flipped-classroom format. You will watch videos and complete in-depth programming assignments and online quizzes at home, then come in to class for advanced discussions and work on projects. This class will culminate in an open-ended final project, which the teaching team will help you on. Prerequisites: Familiarity with programming in Python and Linear Algebra (matrix / vector multiplications). CS 229 may be taken concurrently.

title: Deep Learning for Computer Vision
one: The best-known deep-learning course in computer vision: from kNN to Transformers, with assignments that make you hand-write backpropagation and train CNNs.
pos: CS 231N is the standard entry point to visual recognition and emphasizes the full implement–train–debug loop. Its assignment design (A1–A3 plus a final project) has been borrowed by many courses, and for many people it is the first place a neural network actually runs.
topics: **Image classification**: kNN, linear classifiers, losses and optimization
**CNN architectures**: AlexNet, VGG, ResNet, efficient networks
**Training engineering**: initialization, normalization, regularization, learning rates, data augmentation
**Visualization and interpretability**: saliency maps, feature visualization, adversarial examples
**Detection and segmentation**: R-CNN family, YOLO, semantic/instance segmentation
**Frontier topics**: video, generative models, multimodality, Transformers
**Final project**: usually a real vision task
prereq: Fluency in Python/NumPy; calculus and linear algebra (MATH 19/51); basic probability and statistics (CS 109 level).
assessment: Three programming assignments plus a final project; the workload is heavy but worth it. Check the current syllabus for details.
who: People aiming at CV, multimodality, robot perception, or autonomous driving; engineers who want the low-level implementation skills behind deep learning; prospective vision PhD students.
tips: Hand-write BatchNorm in A2 and the Transformer in A3 instead of copying. For the final project, don't just chase SOTA — a small, well-explained error analysis is more convincing.
description: Computer Vision has become ubiquitous in our society, with applications in search, image understanding, apps, mapping, medicine, drones, and self-driving cars. Core to many of these applications are visual recognition tasks such as image classification and object detection. Recent developments in neural network approaches have greatly advanced the performance of these state-of-the-art visual recognition systems. This course is a deep dive into details of neural-network based deep learning methods for computer vision. During this course, students will learn to implement, train and debug their own neural networks and gain a detailed understanding of cutting-edge research in computer vision. We will cover learning algorithms, neural network architectures, and practical engineering tricks for training and fine-tuning networks for visual recognition tasks.Prerequisites: Proficiency in Python - All class assignments will be in Python (and use numpy) (we provide a tutorial here for those who aren't as familiar with Python). If you have a lot of programming experience but in a different language (e.g. C/C++/Matlab/Javascript) you will probably be fine.College Calculus, Linear Algebra (e.g. MATH 19, MATH 51) -You should be comfortable taking derivatives and understanding matrix vector operations and notation. Basic Probability and Statistics (e.g. CS 109 or other stats course) -You should know basics of probabilities, gaussian distributions, mean, standard deviation, etc.

title: Natural Language Processing with Deep Learning (LINGUIST 284, SYMSYS 195N)
one: The core NLP course from word2vec to LLMs: implement word2vec, RNNs, and attention, then build an LLM project.
pos: CS 224N is Stanford's flagship NLP course and the first stop into LLMs for many people. It starts with word representations and language models, then moves to Transformers, pre-training, fine-tuning, and RLHF, combining mathematical derivations with substantial implementation.
topics: **Pre-trained models**: BERT, GPT, T5, scaling laws
**Adaptation and alignment**: fine-tuning, prompting, RLHF, DPO
**NLP tasks**: syntax, semantics, QA, machine translation, information extraction
**Final project**: usually an LLM/agent research or application project
prereq: Calculus and linear algebra; one of CS 124, CS 221, or CS 229.
assessment: Typically 4–5 assignments plus a midterm and a final project; the assignments involve substantial PyTorch implementation. Check the current syllabus for details.
who: Required for NLP/LLM; people working on agents, RAG, alignment, or multimodal language models; engineers moving from classical NLP to LLMs.
tips: Take CS 229 first, or at least understand softmax, cross-entropy, and backpropagation. If you want to train LLMs from scratch, follow this with CS 336.
description: Methods for processing human language information and the underlying computational properties of natural languages. Focus on deep learning approaches: understanding, implementing, training, debugging, visualizing, and extending neural network models for a variety of language understanding tasks. Exploration of natural language tasks ranging from simple word level and syntactic processing to coreference, question answering, and machine translation. Examination of representative papers and systems and completion of a final project applying a complex neural network model to a large-scale NLP problem. Prerequisites: calculus and linear algebra; CS124, CS221, or CS229.

title: Reinforcement Learning
one: The core reinforcement learning course: MDPs, value iteration, policy gradients, exploration, with deep RL in the assignments.
pos: CS 234 covers the main line of RL from tabular methods to deep RL, with an emphasis on how autonomous systems make decisions through trial and error. It fits sequential decision-making in robotics, games, recommendation, and healthcare, and is a prerequisite for CS 224R/CS 332.
topics: **MDP basics**: returns, Bellman equations, policy evaluation
**Model-free methods**: Monte Carlo, TD, Q-learning, SARSA
**Deep RL and offline RL**: stability issues in practice
**Project**: usually train an agent on a control or game task
prereq: Fluent Python; CS 229 or equivalent ML background; linear algebra and probability.
assessment: Typically 3–4 assignments plus a midterm and a project; at least one deep RL assignment. Check the current syllabus for details.
who: Robotics, RL research, game AI, and recommender systems; anyone working on embodied AI.
tips: Master MDPs and dynamic programming before deep RL. For the exploration part, read Chapters 2–3 of Sutton & Barto.
description: To realize the dreams and impact of AI requires autonomous systems that learn to make good decisions. Reinforcement learning is one powerful paradigm for doing so, and it is relevant to an enormous range of tasks, including robotics, game playing, consumer modeling and healthcare. This class will briefly cover background on Markov decision processes and reinforcement learning, before focusing on some of the central problems, including scaling up to large domains and the exploration challenge. One key tool for tackling complex RL domains is deep learning and this class will include at least one homework on deep reinforcement learning. Prerequisites: proficiency in python, CS 229 or equivalents or permission of the instructor; linear algebra, basic probability.
note: Not offered in the 2026–27 ExploreCourses listing; this page is based on the most recent offering.

title: Deep Generative Models
one: A theory course on deep generative models: the probabilistic foundations and training algorithms behind VAEs, GANs, flows, and diffusion.
pos: CS 236 is one of the most systematic courses on generative modeling, taught by Stefano Ermon. It starts from probabilistic modeling and variational inference and covers VAEs, GANs, normalizing flows, energy-based models, and diffusion/score matching; the math load is high.
topics: **Probability foundations**: maximum likelihood, variational inference, ELBO, MCMC
**GANs**: adversarial training, mode collapse, Wasserstein GAN
**Flow models**: invertible transforms, Jacobians, continuous flows
prereq: At least one of CS 221/228/229/230; probability and calculus; Python programming.
assessment: Assignments plus a midterm/final and a project; both derivations and implementation matter. Check the current syllabus for details.
who: People working on diffusion models, image/video generation, or generative AI research; anyone who wants the probabilistic ideas behind VAEs and GANs.
tips: Brush up on variational inference and score matching first, or the diffusion part will be rough. Pair with CS 236G for the engineering details of GANs.
description: Generative models are widely used in many subfields of AI and Machine Learning. Recent advances in parameterizing these models using neural networks, combined with progress in stochastic optimization methods, have enabled scalable modeling of complex, high-dimensional data including images, text, and speech. In this course, we will study the probabilistic foundations and learning algorithms for deep generative models, including Variational Autoencoders (VAE), Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN), and flow models. The course will also discuss application areas that have benefitted from deep generative models, including computer vision, speech and natural language processing, and reinforcement learning. Prerequisites: Basic knowledge about machine learning from at least one of CS 221, 228, 229 or 230. Students will work with computational and mathematical models and should have a basic knowledge of probabilities and calculus. Proficiency in some programming language, preferably Python, required.

title: Probabilistic Graphical Models: Principles and Techniques
one: A systematic course on probabilistic graphical models: representation, inference, and learning — the foundation for Bayesian methods and structured prediction.
pos: CS 228 is the classic PGM course, covering Bayesian and Markov networks, HMMs, exact and approximate inference, and parameter/structure learning. Its way of encoding uncertainty with graph structure has long-term value for NLP, computational biology, causal inference, and robotics.
topics: **Representation**: Bayesian networks, Markov networks, factor graphs
**Exact inference**: variable elimination, belief propagation, junction trees
**Approximate inference**: variational inference, MCMC, importance sampling
**Applications**: speech, biology, medical diagnosis, vision, robot planning
prereq: Basic probability; algorithm design and analysis.
assessment: Assignments plus a midterm and a project; a mix of math and implementation. Check the current syllabus for details.
who: People working on probabilistic modeling, causality, or Bayesian deep learning; researchers in NLP, computational biology, or robotics who need to handle uncertainty.
tips: It complements CS 229: 229 is prediction-oriented, 228 is about structured uncertainty. Derive variable elimination and VI by hand once.
description: Probabilistic graphical modeling languages for representing complex domains, algorithms for reasoning using these representations, and learning these representations from data. Topics include: Bayesian and Markov networks, extensions to temporal modeling such as hidden Markov models and dynamic Bayesian networks, exact and approximate probabilistic inference algorithms, and methods for learning models from data. Also included are sample applications to various domains including speech recognition, biological modeling and discovery, medical diagnosis, message encoding, vision, and robot motion planning. Prerequisites: basic probability theory and algorithm design and analysis.
note: Not offered in the 2026–27 ExploreCourses listing.

title: Machine Learning Theory (STATS 214)
one: Machine learning theory: generalization bounds, non-convex optimization, and implicit regularization — why deep learning works.
pos: CS 229M (STATS 214) is the most mathematically demanding ML course, aimed at graduate students who want to do theory. It does not teach model tuning; it trains you to analyze modern large-scale nonlinear models with concentration inequalities, uniform convergence, and optimization theory.
topics: **Generalization theory**: uniform convergence, VC dimension, Rademacher complexity
**Non-convex optimization**: gradient descent, saddle points, landscape
**Implicit regularization**: overparameterization, double descent, margin stability
**Unsupervised learning and domain adaptation**: representation learning theory
**Modern model analysis**: approximation and generalization of Transformers/deep networks
prereq: MATH 51; STATS 117; CS 229 or STATS 315A.
assessment: Assignments plus a final/project, mostly proofs and paper reading. Check the current syllabus for details.
who: People who want to do ML theory, a PhD, or rigorous analysis; also suitable for math/statistics backgrounds moving into ML.
tips: Brush up on real analysis and probability first. Don't expect to understand it in one pass — work through the notes and papers repeatedly.
description: How do we use mathematical thinking to design better machine learning methods? This course focuses on developing mathematical tools for answering this question. This course will cover fundamental concepts and principled algorithms in machine learning, particularly those that are related to modern large-scale non-linear models. The topics include concentration inequalities, generalization bounds via uniform convergence, non-convex optimization, implicit regularization effect in deep learning, and unsupervised learning and domain adaptations. Prerequisites: MATH 51 and STATS 117 and either CS 229 or STATS 315A. See https://statistics.stanford.edu/course-equiv for equivalent courses in other departments that satisfy these prerequisites.
note: Not offered in the 2026–27 ExploreCourses listing.

title: Machine Learning with Graphs
one: Graph machine learning: GNNs, knowledge graphs, and influence maximization — turning relational data into learnable representations.
pos: Taught by Jure Leskovec, CS 224W is one of the most popular courses on graph neural networks. It covers graph structure analysis, node/graph representation learning, GNNs, knowledge-graph reasoning, propagation and influence, with applications in social networks, recommendation, biological networks, and fraud detection.
topics: **Graph basics**: centrality, community detection, power laws, graph generation
**Knowledge graphs**: TransE, RotatE, querying and reasoning
**Propagation and influence**: independent cascade, linear threshold, influence maximization
**Graph generation and self-supervision**: graph contrastive learning, diffusion
**Project**: usually prediction/analysis on real graph data
prereq: CS 109; one introductory machine learning course.
assessment: Assignments plus a project; programming is mainly PyTorch/PyG. Check the current syllabus for details.
who: Social networks, recommendation, risk control, biological networks, and knowledge graphs; anyone who wants to model non-Euclidean data.
tips: Understand the message-passing paradigm before learning GNN variants. The project can build on CS 246's large-scale data methods.
description: Many complex data can be represented as a graph of relationships between objects. Such networks are a fundamental tool for modeling complex social, technological, and biological systems. This course focuses on the computational, algorithmic, and modeling challenges specific to the analysis of massive graphs. By means of studying the underlying graph structure and its features, students are introduced to machine learning techniques and data mining tools apt to reveal insights on a variety of networks. Topics include: representation learning and Graph Neural Networks; algorithms for the World Wide Web; reasoning over Knowledge Graphs; influence maximization; disease outbreak detection, social network analysis. Prerequisites: CS109, any introductory course in Machine Learning.

title: Agentic AI
one: Turn LLMs into agents that can retrieve, reason, and execute long-horizon tasks: RAG, tools, knowledge bases, formal methods, and long-range planning.
pos: CS 224V is a project-based agentic AI course with hard-core lectures, taught by Yuhao He and others. It is not about calling APIs; it systematically discusses agent reliability: reducing hallucination, mixing structured and unstructured knowledge, using formal methods to guarantee decisions, and optimizing long-horizon tasks.
topics: **RAG and task formalization**: retrieval augmentation, formal task descriptions, reducing hallucination
**Hybrid knowledge reasoning**: joint reasoning over databases, knowledge bases, and unstructured text
**AI-driven knowledge curation**: organizing and discovering knowledge in scientific discovery
**Formal methods**: improving the accuracy and interpretability of decision-making agents
**Long-horizon agents**: automatically optimizing accuracy and efficiency on long tasks
**Quarter-long project**: method research or a domain agent
prereq: One of LINGUIST 180/280, CS 124, CS 224N, CS 224S, or CS 224U.
assessment: Lectures plus a quarter-long project that carries most of the grade (research or application). Check the current syllabus for details.
who: People who want to do agent research, AI scientists, or domain automation; anyone who knows LLM basics and wants to go deeper on reliability and formal guarantees.
tips: Get familiar with ReAct, Toolformer, RAG, and function calling first. Pick a quantifiable task for the project, or evaluation will be hard.
description: AI agents powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) are already transforming how we work, learn, and solve problems - and we are only at the beginning. As these systems grow more capable, they hold extraordinary promise for accelerating scientific discovery and democratizing access to high-quality medical, legal, and educational services worldwide. This is a project course coupled with rigorous lectures on the principles, methodologies, and cutting-edge research underlying agentic AI. Students undertake a substantial quarter-long project in either foundational methodology research or building novel agents in a domain of their choice. Topics covered include: (1) minimizing hallucination in question-answering and task-oriented agents using Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and formal task descriptions; (2) hybrid knowledge reasoning over databases, knowledge bases, and unstructured text; (3) AI-driven knowledge curation and discovery for scientific research; (4) improving the accuracy and interpretability of decision-making agents through formal methods; and (5) automated techniques for improving the accuracy and efficiency of long-horizon agents. Prerequisites: one of LINGUIST 180/280, CS 124, CS 224N, CS 224S, or CS 224U.

title: Engineering AI Agents
one: Engineering methodology from LLM pipelines to compound AI systems to autonomous agents: choose the problem, decompose it, pick components, and evaluate.
pos: CS 329Z is one of the closest courses to the AI engineer role, taught by Diyi Yang and others. It emphasizes that an agent is not one model but a compound system of LLMs, retrievers, tools, and optimizers; students build RAG, tool use, and an agent loop from scratch, then move to frameworks such as DSPy.
topics: **Compound AI systems**: design patterns for multi-component systems
**Tool use**: function calling, tool selection, error handling
**Agent loop**: planning, execution, reflection, termination conditions
**DSPy**: declarative optimization of prompts and pipelines
**Data curation and evaluation**: building eval sets, offline/online metrics
**Three applied homework assignments + a quarter-long project**
prereq: Programming ability; LLM basics (prompting, API use); ML background is a plus.
assessment: Three fully applied homework assignments plus a quarter-long project, focused on building, optimizing, and evaluating. Check the current syllabus for details.
who: Aspiring AI engineers/agent engineers; people moving from backend/ML to LLM applications; founders.
tips: It complements CS 224V: 224V is research/formal, 329Z is engineering/eval. Don't just get the demo running — make the evaluation solid.
description: The shift from monolithic language models to compound AI systems - systems with multiple interacting components including LLMs, retrievers, tools, and optimizers -n represents a fundamental change in how AI applications are built for people. This course teaches students how to engineer agentic systems: the full spectrum from simple LLM pipelines to compound AI systems to autonomous agents. Students will learn to pick what types of problems to focus on, decompose problems, select appropriate components, collect and curate data, build evaluations, and reason about the design tradeoffs that arise when building these systems in practice. Students first build core components (RAG, tool use, agent loops) from scratch, then learn how frameworks like DSPy abstract these patterns. Through three fully applied homework assignments and a quarter-long project, students will gain hands-on experience building, optimizing, and evaluating agentic systems.
instructors: Yang, D.; Ryan, M.; Yang, J.

title: Self Improving AI Agents
one: A research seminar on self-improvement, verifiers, test-time compute, search, tools, multimodal web, and long-horizon planning.
pos: CS 329A is taught by Anmol Chowdhery and Azalia Mirhoseini and focuses on how agents keep improving through interaction with the environment and themselves. The course is mainly paper discussion and an original research project, with academic and industry speakers; it suits people who have already decided to do agent research.
topics: **Verifiers and search**: learned verifiers, best-of-n, tree search
**Test-time compute**: inference-time scaling, chain-of-thought, parallel sampling
**Tools and retrieval**: tool use, retrieval, multimodal web interaction
**Multi-step reasoning and planning**: long-horizon decomposition, orchestration frameworks
**Evaluation and orchestration**: robust eval, failure modes
**Applications**: coding agents, STEM research assistants, robotics
prereq: CS 224N or CS 229S; fluent Python and LLM APIs.
assessment: Paper reading/discussion plus an original research project and speaker lectures. Check the current syllabus for details.
who: Graduate students interested in agent research, alignment, or reasoning/planning; people with some LLM experience.
tips: Read ReAct, Reflexion, Tree of Thoughts, and Self-Rewarding LM first. The project needs a clear baseline and evaluation.
description: This graduate seminar course covers the latest techniques and applications of AI agents that can continuously improve themselves through interaction with themselves and the environment. The course will start with self-improvement techniques for LLMs, such as constitutional AI, using learned/domain-specific verifiers, scaling test-time compute, and combining search with LLMs. We will then discuss the latest research in augmenting LLMs with tool use and retrieval techniques, and orchestrating AI capabilities with multimodal web interaction. We will next discuss multi-step reasoning and planning problems for agentic workflows, and the challenges in building robust evaluation and orchestration frameworks. Industry applications that will be discussed include coding agents, research assistants in STEM, robotics and more. Students will work on an original research project in this area, discuss the suggested readings in each class, and learn from invited academic and industry speakers. Prerequisites: CS224N or CS229S; Fluency in Python programming and using large language model APIs.

title: Machine Learning from Human Preferences
one: The theory and practice of RLHF: from choice models and preference learning to assistance games and fairness.
pos: Taught by Sanmi Koyejo, CS 329H systematically explains how to optimize systems that are used by people. It connects psychometrics, discrete choice, reinforcement learning, information retrieval, and normative theory — a rigorous course for understanding RLHF/DPO and preference modeling in recommender systems.
topics: **Choice modeling**: random utility, Plackett-Luce, axiomatic approaches
**Imitation and active learning**: behavior cloning, preference queries
**Behavioral biases and style control**: preference heterogeneity, prompt/style
**Aggregation and fairness**: social choice, aggregating group preferences
prereq: Graduate-level ML (CS 229 level); probability and optimization.
assessment: Assignments plus a project/paper reproduction, combining theory and experiments. Check the current syllabus for details.
who: Researchers in alignment, RLHF, recommendation, or HCI; engineers who want to understand why preference data is hard.
tips: Understand Bradley-Terry and PPO first. Pair it with the RLHF chapter of CS 224N.
description: Machine learning from human preferences (MLHP) provides mechanisms for optimizing systems that are used by humans - with applications in personalization, finetuning, and assistance. MLHP has been important to successes in modern language modeling, but the technical and conceptual underpinnings are spread across fields: psychometrics, discrete choice, reinforcement learning, information retrieval, and normative theory. This course will provide a careful and practical introduction to the main methods and models of MLHP. It will cover: choice modeling and its axiomatic approaches; imitation and static and active learning of choice; reinforcement learning from human feedback; assistance games, bandits, and recommendation; behavioral biases, style control; aggregation and fairness. This is a graduate-level course. By the end of the course, students should be able to build, analyze, and optimize systems that are used by humans.

title: Language Modeling from Scratch
one: Build a language model from scratch: data cleaning, tokenizer, Transformer, training, scaling, evaluation, and deployment.
pos: CS 336 is one of the most hard-core LLM courses, taught by Percy Liang and Tatsunori Hashimoto. Inspired by 'build an OS from scratch', it walks through the full language-model lifecycle; the assignments need substantial GPU compute, and enrollment requires an application.
topics: **Model**: Transformer architecture, attention variants, positional encoding
**Training**: initialization, optimizers, learning rates, mixed precision, distributed training
**Safety and ethics**: data copyright, bias, misuse
prereq: Strong programming; deep learning background (CS 224N/CS 231N/CS 230 level); application required, GPU resources recommended.
assessment: Typically about five programming assignments that build the LM step by step, plus a project; compute-heavy. Check the current syllabus for details.
who: People who want to understand the full LLM stack and later work on pre-training/inference/systems; founders building models.
tips: Take CS 224N or CS 231N first. Without GPUs you can run small models, but the assignment experience will be limited.
description: Language models serve as the cornerstone of modern natural language processing (NLP) applications and open up a new paradigm of having a single general purpose system address a range of downstream tasks. As the field of artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and NLP continues to grow, possessing a deep understanding of language models becomes essential for scientists and engineers alike. This course is designed to provide students with a comprehensive understanding of language models by walking them through the entire process of developing their own. Drawing inspiration from operating systems courses that create an entire operating system from scratch, we will lead students through every aspect of language model creation, including data collection and cleansing for pre-training, transformer model construction, model training, and evaluation before deployment. Application required, apply at http://cs336.stanford.edu/

title: Advances in Foundation Models
one: A panorama of foundation models: models/algorithms, systems/infrastructure, ethics/social impact, plus a hands-on project.
pos: CS 324 is a foundation-model course launched in 2023, covering the principles, systems, and social impact of models such as GPT-3, CLIP, and Stable Diffusion. It has industry speakers and emphasizes projects over derivations; it suits people who want a fast, broad view of FMs.
topics: **Ethics and social impact**: bias, copyright, misuse, regulation
**Quarter-long project**: study FM capabilities or build an application
prereq: Deep learning background (CS 224N/CS 230/CS 231N level).
assessment: Mainly a quarter-long final project, possibly with assignments/reading. Check the current syllabus for details.
who: Product/research/strategy people who want to understand the FM ecosystem; students looking for FM application directions.
tips: The content leans 2023; combine it with recent papers. Pick a narrow, deep problem for the project.
description: Foundation models (FMs) are transforming the landscape of AI in research and industry. Such models (e.g., GPT-3, CLIP, Stable Diffusion) are trained on large amounts of broad data and are adaptable to a wide range of downstream tasks. In this course, students will learn fundamentals behind the models and algorithms, systems and infrastructure, and ethics and societal impacts of foundation models, with an emphasis on gaining hands-on experience and identifying real-world use-cases for FMs. Students will hear from speakers in industry working on foundation models in the wild. The main class assignment will be a quarter-long final project, involving either researching the capabilities of FMs or building an FM-powered application.
note: Not offered in the 2026–27 ExploreCourses listing; the link points to the 2023 winter course materials.

title: Transformers United V6 (SYMSYS 25)
one: The public lecture series of the Transformer universe: one top researcher each week on LLMs, generation, robotics, and science.
pos: CS 25 is one of Stanford's most popular 1-unit seminars, with speakers from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, NVIDIA, and elsewhere. There are no assignments — attendance is enough — and lectures are streamed and recorded, making it a fast way to scan the frontier.
prereq: Basic deep learning and Transformer knowledge (understand attention), or CS 224N/CS 231N/CS 230.
assessment: 1 unit, S/NC, attendance only; no assignments.
who: Anyone — students, engineers, and researchers who want a low-cost way to track the frontier; also useful as group-meeting or course supplementary material.
tips: You can watch the YouTube recordings without enrolling. Write down three takeaways per talk, or you will forget them.
description: Since their introduction in 2017, Transformers have revolutionized Deep Learning, powering large language models (LLM) like ChatGPT and DeepSeek, image and video generation (e.g. Dall-E and Sora), and much more. In CS25, one of Stanford's hottest seminar courses, we delve into Transformer architectures and their diverse applications through classroom discussions and instructor and guest lectures. Topics include LLM, creative uses in art and music, healthcare, neuroscience, robotics, and so forth. We host leading researchers, with past speakers like Andrej Karpathy, Geoffrey Hinton, Jim Fan, Ashish Vaswani, and folks from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, NVIDIA, etc. Lectures are livestreamed and recorded, attracting a global audience with over a million total YouTube views. This is a 1-unit S/NC course, where attendance is the only homework! Enroll via Axess or audit through livestreams or in-person, space permitting. Prerequisites: basic Deep Learning and Transformers knowledge (understanding of attention) or completion of CS224N, CS231N, or CS230. Course website: https://web.stanford.edu/class/cs25/
note: CS 25 is not offered in the 2026–27 ExploreCourses listing; the cross-listed SYMSYS 25 is offered in Spring 2027. CS 25 has run many times before, and lecture recordings are on YouTube.

title: Mechanistic Interpretability
one: Mechanistic interpretability: probing, steering, causal abstraction, and sparse autoencoders — understanding what a model is actually computing.
pos: Taught by Thomas Icard, CS 221M is one of the few courses that systematically teaches mechanistic interpretability. It emphasizes causal methods rather than 'looking at pictures', covering probing, steering, causal abstraction, SAEs, and circuits, with guest lectures from academic and industry interpretability labs.
topics: **Steering**: activation interventions, direction vectors, causal tracing
**Causal abstraction**: causal graphs, interventions, abstraction mappings
**Sparse autoencoders**: dictionary learning, feature decomposition, monosemanticity
**Interpretability and safety**: using it for auditing and alignment
prereq: Deep learning/LLM basics; probability and linear algebra; having read about Transformers helps.
assessment: Assignments plus a project/paper reproduction; research- and discussion-oriented. Check the current syllabus for details.
who: People who want to do interpretability, AI safety, or model auditing; researchers who want to understand LLM internals.
tips: Read Anthropic's 'Towards Monosemanticity' and 'Scaling Monosemanticity' first, plus the causal-abstraction papers.
description: What is the internal structure of modern neural networks and how can we study it? This course provides a broad and deep introduction to interpretability, the subfield of machine learning concerned with understanding precisely how models process information and why they produce the outputs they do. We will cover topics such as probing, steering, causal abstraction, and sparse autoencoders, with a particular emphasis on causal methods and large language models. The course will include guest lectures from leading interpretability labs across academia and industry.

zh: 可信机器学习：构建与评估 Agent 系统
title: Trustworthy Machine Learning: Building and evaluating agentic systems
one: Trustworthy agent systems: build a prototype, then use evaluation to make it reliable.
pos: CS 329T is a project-based course on the theme 'prototypes are easy, reliability is hard'. It covers foundation models, prompting, RAG, and agentic architectures, with an evaluation method for each; students finish with an evaluation-driven trustworthy agent application.
topics: **FMs and prompting**: capability boundaries, prompt patterns
**Evaluation**: offline metrics, LLM-as-judge, human evaluation, red teaming
**Team project**: build and evaluate an agent application
prereq: CS 229 or an equivalent Python ML course; deep learning (CS 230/CS 231N); familiarity with scikit-learn/Keras.
assessment: Intro assignments (RAG/agent) plus a team project and an evaluation report. Check the current syllabus for details.
who: People who want to build agent products, AI evaluation, or trustworthy AI; anyone who can build a demo and wants evaluation methodology.
tips: Pair with CS 329Z: 329Z is more full-stack engineering, 329T is more trust + evaluation. Define metrics before writing code.
description: This project-based course will introduce students to building and evaluating agentic AI applications powered by foundation models. The overriding theme of the course is that building an initial prototype AI system can often be completed easily but refining a prototype into something that is useful and reliable requires iterative improvement based on clear evaluation metrics. We will cover background in foundation models, prompting, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) before introducing full agentic AI architectures. For each architecture, the course will study methods for evaluation. Students will complete introductory homework assignments to become familiar with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and agentic AI. Students will then work in pairs or small teams to develop applications using agentic or other approaches and evaluate them by adapting evaluation methods presented in the class.Prerequisites: CS229 or similar introductory Python-based ML class; knowledge of deep learning such as CS230, CS231N; familiarity with ML frameworks in Python (scikit-learn, Keras) assumed.
note: Not offered in the 2026–27 ExploreCourses listing.

title: Apps With LLMs Inside
one: LLM application development: ship apps in sprints and understand model capability boundaries and the new programming paradigm.
pos: CS 224G is a project course that treats the LLM as a new CPU and explores how to build applications around it. It runs in two-week sprints with industry guest lectures, and suits people who want to ship a demo quickly.
topics: **LLM capabilities and limits**: hallucination, context, cost
**Tools and retrieval**: function calling, RAG, external APIs
**Application architecture**: frontend, backend, streaming, state management
prereq: Programming ability; basic ML/LLM awareness; no research background required.
assessment: Two-week sprint assignments plus a final project and guest lectures. Check the current syllabus for details.
who: People who want to build LLM products or startups; product managers, designers, full-stack engineers.
tips: It complements CS 329Z: 224G is product cadence, 329Z is systems and eval. Define the user problem before choosing a model.
description: With ChatGPT, neural networks have had their Lisp moment. Conversation has become code and the model is the CPU for this ultimate programming language. A new universe of App development has opened up, and there are no guides for it, yet. This is a project course designed to explore the space of Apps built around LLMs, starting by playing with them, learning their limitations, and then applying a set of techniques to program them efficiently and effectively. Assignments are due on a two week "sprint" cadence to mimic a startup style environment. Guest lectures by area experts provide industry perspective.

zh: AGI 的推理、规划与决策
title: Artificial General Intelligence for Reasoning, Planning, and Decision Making
one: Reasoning, planning, and decision-making for AGI: from System 1 to System 2, multi-LLM collaboration, and temporal reasoning.
pos: Taught by Edward Chang, CS 372 is a research-oriented course on moving LLMs from pattern matching to deliberate reasoning and planning. It covers multi-LLM collaboration, entropy-guided information exchange, constitutional AI, and temporal reasoning, with healthcare as an application case.
topics: **System 1 vs System 2**: intuition and deliberate reasoning
**Multi-LLM collaboration**: the MACI framework, role division, debate
**Temporal reasoning and planning**: time awareness, long-horizon tasks
prereq: Machine learning and deep learning basics.
assessment: Lectures/discussion plus a hands-on project. Check the current syllabus for details.
who: Graduate students interested in AGI, reasoning, planning, and multi-agent systems; people comfortable with speculative material.
tips: Listen critically: some concepts (such as 'consciousness') are contested. Focus on verifiable reasoning and planning methods.
description: Course Description:Large Language Models (LLMs) have revolutionized AI through remarkable pattern matching capabilities. However, the path to Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) requires advancing beyond unconscious (System 1) to conscious (System 2) processing. This research-oriented course explores fundamental approaches to elevate LLMs toward AGI capabilities through conscious reasoning, planning, and decision-making. Core Research Questions: 1. How can we enable LLMs to transition from pattern matching to conscious deliberation? 2. What frameworks support robust reasoning and verifiable decisions? 3. How do we implement planning and temporal awareness in LLM systems? 4. What role does multi-LLM agent collaboration play in advancing toward AGI capabilities? The course examines: 1. Theoretical foundations of consciousness in AI 2. Multi-LLM Agent Collaborative Intelligence (MACI) frameworks 3. Entropy-guided information exchange 4. Constitutional AI principles 5. Temporal reasoning and planning architectures. Through lectures, discussions, and hands-on projects, students will explore practical implementations across various domains. While healthcare provides immediate applications (diagnosis, treatment planning), the principles apply broadly to any field requiring AGI-level reasoning capabilities. Prerequisites: Machine Learning, Deep Learning
note: Not offered in the 2026–27 ExploreCourses listing; no stable course-site link found.

title: AI Agents and Simulations (PSYCH 186)
one: Simulate human society with agent-based models and generative agents, and run 'what if' experiments.
pos: Taught by Michael Bernstein and Noah Goodman, CS 222 spans social science, behavioral science, and generative AI. It moves from classical agent-based modeling to LLM-driven generative agents, discussing how to simulate individuals and societies, how to evaluate simulation fidelity, and the ethical issues involved.
topics: **Social simulation**: opinion spread, cooperation, public policy
**Ethics**: manipulation, privacy, the power of simulation
prereq: Python programming; AI (CS 221/224), human-centered design, or social psychology helps but is not required.
assessment: Mainly a team project plus assignments/discussion. Check the current syllabus for details.
who: Computational social science, multi-agent systems, AI policy/ethics; anyone who wants to build social simulations or generative agents.
tips: Read Generative Agents (Park et al., 2023) and classic Schelling/NetLogo models first. Pay attention to reproducibility and ethical boundaries.
description: How might we craft simulations of human societies that reflect our lives? Many of the greatest challenges of our time, from encouraging healthy public discourse to designing pandemic responses, and building global cooperation for sustainability, must reckon with the complex nature of our world. The power to simulate hypothetical worlds in which we can ask "what if" counterfactual questions, and paint concrete pictures of how a multiverse of different possibilities might unfold, promises an opportunity to navigate this complexity. This course presents a tour of multiple decades of effort in social, behavioral, and computational sciences to simulate individuals and their societies, starting from foundational literature in agent-based modeling to generative agents that leverage the power of the most advanced generative AI to create high-fidelity simulations. Along the way, students will learn about the opportunities, challenges, and ethical considerations in the field of human behavioral simulations. Prerequisites: Team projects and some course assignments will involve programming in Python. Having a background in human-centered design (e.g., CS 147, ME 115A, or a class from the d.school), AI (e.g., CS 221, CS 224), or social psychology may be helpful, although it is not required.

title: Systems for Machine Learning
one: ML systems: efficiency across the data, training, and inference stack, with hardware-software co-design.
pos: CS 229S looks at machine learning from a systems perspective: models are bigger, data is larger, hardware is more heterogeneous — where is the performance bottleneck? It covers data pipelines, distributed training, GPUs/accelerators, networking, inference serving, and compilation, for people who want to work on MLSys/infrastructure.
topics: **Distributed training**: data, model, and pipeline parallelism
**Inference serving**: batching, scheduling, KV cache, latency
**Cases and project**: performance analysis of real systems
prereq: CS 224N or CS 229; systems/architecture background helps.
assessment: Assignments plus a project, focused on systems implementation and performance analysis. Check the current syllabus for details.
who: People who want to work on MLSys, inference infrastructure, or training platforms; systems people moving into ML.
tips: Pair with CS 149 (parallel computing) and CS 217 (accelerators). Understand the roofline model and communication costs first.
description: Deep learning and neural networks are being increasingly adopted across industries. They are now used to serve billions of users across applications such as search, knowledge discovery, and productivity assistants. As models become more capable and intelligent, this trend of large-scale adoption will continue to grow rapidly. Due to the widespread application, there is an increasing need to achieve high performance for both training and serving deep-learning models. However, performance is hindered by a multitude of infrastructure and lifecycle hurdles - the increasing complexity of the models, massive sizes of training and inference data, heterogeneity of the available accelerators and multi-node platforms, and diverse network properties. The slow adaptation of systems to new algorithms creates a bottleneck for the rapid evolution of deep-learning models and their applications. This course will cover systems approaches for improving the efficiency of machine learning pipelines - comprising data preparation, model training, and model deployment & inference -at each level of the systems stack spanning software and hardware. Pre-req: CS224N or CS229.
note: Not offered in the 2026–27 ExploreCourses listing; no stable course-site link found.

title: Machine Learning Systems Design
one: ML systems design: from data management to deployment and monitoring, plus privacy, fairness, and security.
pos: CS 329S is a project-based ML systems course about the engineering beyond the model: managing data, choosing models, scaling training, monitoring production, and coordinating teams. It also covers privacy, fairness, and security — the real-world issues every system faces.
topics: **Data engineering**: data management, labeling, versioning, quality
**Training and scaling**: distributed systems, cost, experiment management
**People and society**: privacy, fairness, security, teamwork
**Project**: design and implement an ML system
prereq: At least one of CS 229/230/231N/224N; familiarity with one framework (PyTorch/TF/JAX).
assessment: Mainly a project plus assignments/reading. Check the current syllabus for details.
who: ML engineers moving from model tuning to systems; researchers who want engineering skills; technical product managers.
tips: Pair with 'Designing Machine Learning Systems'. The project should include monitoring and rollback, not just a model.
description: This project-based course covers the iterative process for designing, developing, and deploying machine learning systems. It focuses on systems that require massive datasets and compute resources, such as large neural networks. Students will learn about data management, data engineering, approaches to model selection, training, scaling, how to continually monitor and deploy changes to ML systems, as well as the human side of ML projects. In the process, students will learn about important issues including privacy, fairness, and security. Pre-requisites: At least one of the following; CS229, CS230, CS231N, CS224N or equivalent. Students should have a good understanding of machine learning algorithms and should be familiar with at least one framework such as TensorFlow, PyTorch, JAX.
note: Not offered in the 2026–27 ExploreCourses listing; the link points to the course materials site.

title: AI Inference Infrastructure
one: AI inference infrastructure: how compound AI systems are deployed, scheduled, and scaled in the cloud.
pos: Taught by Christos Kozyrakis, CS 349D is a research seminar focused on inference rather than training. It argues that future AI systems are compound systems (multiple models + retrieval + tools + traditional software) and discusses the cloud infrastructure, scheduling, and architecture patterns that support them.
topics: **Inference serving**: batching, continuous batching, KV cache
**Scheduling and routing**: model routing, priorities, SLAs
**Industry practice**: guest lectures from Databricks, OpenAI, NVIDIA, etc.
prereq: Systems/architecture/ML basics; distributed-systems experience helps.
assessment: Paper discussion plus guest lectures and a 2–3 person team project. Check the current syllabus for details.
who: People who want to work on inference platforms, AI infrastructure, or cloud systems; systems-oriented graduate students.
tips: Pair with CS 349E for single-machine/cluster performance and CS 349F for networking. Base the project on a real serving stack.
description: The emergence of foundation models has revolutionized AI applications, but the most powerful AI systems today are increasingly compound systems - compositions of multiple models, retrievers, tools, and traditional software components. This research seminar explores the intersection of cloud computing infrastructure and compound AI systems, covering both the infrastructure required to build and deploy these systems at scale and the architectural patterns that make them effective. Students will participate in guest lectures from leading experts across academia and industry, including leaders of companies like Databricks, OpenAI, Foundry, NVIDIA, Microsoft, and more, read and discuss papers, and complete a quarter-long project in groups of 2-3.

zh: 大规模高效 ML 推理
title: Efficient ML Inference at Scale (EE 339)
one: Efficient inference at scale: model optimization, distributed serving, AI hardware, kernels, and compilers.
pos: CS 349E (EE 339) is taught by Mark Horowitz, Fredrik Kjolstad, and others — a hard-core mix of systems, algorithms, and hardware. It discusses how to serve large models on heterogeneous machines with low latency, high throughput, and low cost, covering quantization, distributed serving, performance modeling, kernel programming, and AI compilers.
topics: **Model optimization**: quantization, pruning, distillation, speculative decoding
**Distributed serving**: tensor parallelism, pipelines, prefill/decode disaggregation
**AI compilers**: graph optimization, operator selection, code generation
prereq: Computer architecture, operating systems, ML basics; strong programming.
assessment: Assignments plus a project, focused on implementation and measurement. Check the current syllabus for details.
who: Graduate students/engineers working on inference performance, AI chips, or compilers; systems people going deeper into ML.
tips: Brush up on CS 217/CS 149 first. Be ready to run benchmarks, not just read paper numbers.
description: A graduate-level course focused on principles and techniques for designing and building large-scale disaggregated AI inference systems. The course explores architectural, algorithmic, system-level, and kernel implementation techniques for serving models with low latency, high throughput, and low cost on heterogeneous machines. Topics include model optimization techniques, distributed serving, AI hardware and performance modelling, kernel programming, and AI compilers. Class website: cs349e.github.io
instructors: Asgar, Z.; Raina, P.; Horowitz, M.; Kjoelstad, F.

zh: AI 系统的网络 Fabric 架构
title: Fabric Architectures For AI Systems
one: The network fabric of AI clusters: fat trees, congestion control, and scheduling, aiming for ultra-low latency and near-100% goodput.
pos: CS 349F focuses on the interconnect networks of large GPU/CPU clusters and on time-sensitive systems such as financial trading and multiplayer games. It covers data-center fabric architectures, transport protocols, congestion control, load balancing, and scheduling, with industry experts discussing real cluster design and operations.
prereq: CS 144/CS 140 or distributed-systems basics; EE 178 helps.
assessment: 2 units, S/NC; discussion plus a project/case study. Check the current syllabus for details.
who: Networking, clusters, and data centers; anyone working on AI infrastructure.
tips: Read it with CS 349D/E to get the full single-machine, cluster, and network picture.
description: The course is concerned with the design and operation of the network fabrics which interconnect large-scale compute and storage nodes in modern AI GPU clusters, cloud computing systems, and "time-sensitive systems" like financial trading platforms and massive multi-player games. We will consider architectures, protocols and algorithms which enable these network fabrics to deliver deterministic and ultra-low latency at near-100% goodput. Topics include data center fabric architectures - the fat tree topology, transport protocols - congestion control and load balancing, and scheduling algorithms - job scheduling, fabric scheduling and their interaction. A particular focus will be the contrast and synergy between the edge- and network-centric approaches to building high-performance network fabrics. Students will hear from industry experts who design, operate and use large-scale GPU and CPU clusters. Recommended: Knowledge of basic Networking, OS, or Distributed Systems (CS 144, 140, or equivalent), as well as basic EE courses (EE 178) will be useful.
note: Offered in Autumn 2026–27; the official site is restricted, so only the ExploreCourses link is provided.

title: Hardware Accelerators for Machine Learning (EE 244)
one: ML hardware accelerators: dataflow, tensor processing, memory hierarchy, compilation, and mapping CNNs/Transformers.
pos: CS 217 (EE 244) is taught by Olukotun and Tambe and is a classic course on AI chips. It starts from the compute patterns of CNNs/Transformers and covers accelerator architecture, dataflow, memory hierarchy, low precision/sparsity, and compilation, ending with a design project.
topics: **AI compute patterns**: CNNs, Transformers, training vs inference
**Accelerator architecture**: systolic arrays, tensor cores, dataflow
**Memory hierarchy**: on-chip buffers, HBM, data reuse
**Low precision and sparsity**: quantization, pruning, compression
prereq: Digital circuits/computer architecture; VLSI or FPGA experience helps.
assessment: Paper reading plus a final design project. Check the current syllabus for details.
who: People who want to work on AI chips, accelerators, or architecture; hardware people who want to understand ML workloads.
tips: Understand roofline and matrix-multiply tiling first. Pair with CS 149/CS 349E.
description: This course explores the design, programming, and performance of modern AI accelerators. It covers architectural techniques, dataflow, tensor processing, memory hierarchies, compilation for accelerators, and emerging trends in AI computing. This course will cover modern AI/ML algorithms such as convolutional neural nets, and Transformer-based models / LLMs. We will consider both training and inference for these models and discuss the impact of parameters such as batch size, precision, sparsity and compression on the accuracy of these models. Students will become familiar with hardware implementation techniques for using parallelism, locality, and low precision to implement the core computational kernels used in ML. Students will develop intuitions to make system-level trade-offs to design energy-efficient accelerators. Students will read recent research papers and complete a final design project.

zh: 计算机视觉：从 3D 感知到重建
title: Computer Vision: From 3D Perception to 3D Reconstruction and Beyond
one: Computer vision from camera models to 3D reconstruction: geometry first, deep learning second.
pos: CS 231A is the classic course on 3D vision and geometry, complementing CS 231N: 231N leans recognition and deep learning, while 231A leans cameras, projection, stereo, SfM, and 3D understanding. It is more mathematical and geometric, and suits people interested in AR/VR, robotics, and autonomous-driving perception.
topics: **Cameras and projection**: pinhole model, intrinsics/extrinsics, distortion
**Segmentation and clustering**: classical and learned methods
**SfM and SLAM basics**: structure from motion
prereq: Linear algebra; basic probability and statistics; programming.
assessment: Assignments plus a project, including geometric derivations and implementation. Check the current syllabus for details.
who: 3D vision, robotics, AR/VR, and autonomous-driving perception; CV students who want geometry foundations.
tips: Take CS 231N first or concurrently. Derive epipolar geometry and bundle adjustment by hand.
description: (Formerly 223B) An introduction to the concepts and applications in computer vision. Topics include: cameras and projection models, low-level image processing methods such as filtering and edge detection; mid-level vision topics such as segmentation and clustering; shape reconstruction from stereo, as well as high-level vision tasks such as object recognition, scene recognition, face detection and human motion categorization. Prerequisites: linear algebra, basic probability and statistics.
note: Not offered in the 2026–27 ExploreCourses listing.

title: Generative Adversarial Networks
one: A dedicated GAN course: from principles to SOTA, covering training stability, evaluation, and bias.
pos: CS 236G is a special-topics course on generative models focused on GANs. It goes from basic adversarial training to SOTA variants such as StyleGAN, discusses mode collapse, training stability, evaluation metrics, and bias, and covers applications in image editing, medical low-data settings, and climate visualization.
topics: **Training techniques**: WGAN, spectral normalization, TTUR, regularization
prereq: Linear algebra, statistics, CS 106B; a graduate AI course (CS 229/230/221).
assessment: Assignments plus a project. Check the current syllabus for details.
who: Image generation, visual editing, and generative-model engineering; people who want to understand GANs rather than only calling diffusion.
tips: Take CS 236 or CS 231N first. Reproduce a GAN training-stability failure once by hand.
description: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have rapidly emerged as the state-of-the-art technique in realistic image generation. This course presents theoretical intuition and practical knowledge on GANs, from their simplest to their state-of-the-art forms. Their benefits and applications span realistic image editing that is omnipresent in popular app filters, enabling tumor classification under low data schemes in medicine, and visualizing realistic scenarios of climate change destruction. This course also examines key challenges of GANs today, including reliable evaluation, inherent biases, and training stability. After this course, students should be familiar with GANs and the broader generative models and machine learning contexts in which these models are situated. Prerequisites: linear algebra, statistics, CS106B, plus a graduate-level AI course such as: CS230, CS229 (or CS129), or CS221.
note: Not offered in the 2026–27 ExploreCourses listing.

title: Neural Models for 3D Geometry
one: Neural representations for 3D geometry: point clouds, meshes, implicit fields, and 3D generation.
pos: CS 348N studies how to generate and manipulate high-quality 3D models and scenes with machine learning. It covers geometry representations, 3D datasets, point-cloud/mesh networks, neural implicits, 3D generative models, conditional generation, and evaluation — a core course for 3D generation/graphics.
topics: **Geometry representations**: point clouds, meshes, voxels, SDFs, NeRF
prereq: CS 148; deep learning basics; CS 229 recommended.
assessment: Assignments plus a project. Check the current syllabus for details.
who: 3D generation, graphics, AR/VR, and robot simulation.
tips: Learn NeRF and diffusion first, then revisit 3D versions of GAN/VAE. Pair with CS 468.
description: Course Description: Generation of high-quality 3D models and scenes by leveraging machine learning tools and approaches. Survey of geometry representations. Public 3D object and scene data sets. Neural architectures for geometry, including deep architectures for point clouds and meshes. Generative models for 3D: autoencoders, GANs, neural implicits, neural ODEs, autoregressive models. Conditional generation based on images or partial geometry. Variation generation. Evaluation metrics for content generation. Use of synthetic data in ML training pipelines. Prerequisites: CS148 and the rudiments of deep learning. Recommended: CS229.
note: Not offered in the 2026–27 ExploreCourses listing; no stable course-site link found.

zh: AI 时代的计算机图形学
title: Computer Graphics in the Era of AI
one: Computer graphics in the AI era: neural rendering, differentiable rendering, materials/textures, animation, and physics simulation.
pos: CS 348I discusses how deep learning is changing four areas of graphics: rendering, geometry, animation, and imaging. For each problem it presents the classical solution first, then SOTA learned methods, and critically evaluates results and impact — a good fit for graphics + AI.
topics: **Differentiable/neural rendering**: NeRF, Gaussian Splatting, neural rendering
**Materials and lighting**: BRDF estimation, inverse rendering
**Textures and images**: texture synthesis, denoising, super-resolution, shading
prereq: CS 148; CS 231N recommended.
assessment: Programming assignments plus a project. Check the current syllabus for details.
who: Graphics, rendering, 3D generation, and film/game technology.
tips: Brush up on graphics fundamentals (ray tracing, BRDF, rendering equation) first. Pair with CS 348N/CS 468.
description: This course introduces deep learning methods and AI technologies applied to four main areas of Computer Graphics: rendering, geometry, animation, and imaging. We will study a wide range of problems on content creation for images, shapes, and animations, recently advanced by deep learning techniques. For each problem, we will understand its conventional solutions, study the state-of-the-art learning-based approaches, and critically evaluate their results as well as the impacts to researchers and practitioners in Computer Graphics. The topics include differentiable rendering/neural rendering, BRDF estimation, texture synthesis, denoising, procedural modeling, view synthesis, colorization, style transfer, motion synthesis, differentiable physics simulation, and reinforcement learning. Through programming projects and homework, students who successfully complete this course will be able to use neural rendering algorithms for image manipulation, apply neural procedural modeling for shape and scene synthesis, exploit data-driven methods for simulating physical phenomena, and implement policy learning algorithms for creating character animation. Recommended Prerequisites: CS148, CS231N
note: Not offered in the 2026–27 ExploreCourses listing; no stable course-site link found.

zh: 几何计算专题：3D/4D 基础模型
title: Topics in Geometric Computing - 3D and 4D Foundation Models
one: A special-topics course in geometric computing, recently focused on 3D/4D foundation models.
pos: CS 468 is a topics course whose content changes each offering; past years covered geometric matching, surface reconstruction, collision detection, computational topology, computer differential geometry, data-driven shape analysis, and non-Euclidean machine learning. Recent offerings shifted to 3D/4D foundation models; it suits graduate students with a geometry/graphics background.
topics: **Surface reconstruction**: point clouds to meshes, implicit representations
**Computational topology**: persistent homology, topological data analysis
**3D/4D foundation models**: multimodal 3D representations, dynamic scenes
prereq: Graphics/geometry/vision background; programming and mathematical maturity.
assessment: Paper discussion plus a project/reproduction. Check the current syllabus for details.
who: Graduate students in 3D vision, graphics, or geometry processing; people interested in 3D foundation models.
tips: Take CS 148/CS 231A first. Topics change every year; read the current syllabus before enrolling.
description: Contents of this course vary with each offering. Past offerings have included geometric matching, surface reconstruction, collision detection, computational topology, differential geometry for computer scientists, computational symmetry and regularity, data-driven shape analysis, and non-Euclidean methods in machine learning.
note: Not offered in the 2026–27 ExploreCourses listing.

title: Computational Imaging (EE 367)
one: Computational imaging: from convolution/denoising to inverse problems, wave optics, and end-to-end optics-algorithm co-design.
pos: CS 448I (EE 367) is taught by Gordon Wetzstein and is a core course in computational photography/imaging. It combines classical image processing, convex optimization, and modern AI, covering denoising, deconvolution, single-pixel imaging, ToF, wave optics, and end-to-end joint optimization of optics and algorithms.
topics: **CNNs for imaging**: image restoration, learned priors
prereq: Signal/image processing/optimization basics; Python programming.
assessment: Assignments plus a term project, emphasizing implementation. Check the current syllabus for details.
who: Computational photography, imaging systems, AR/VR, and microscopy/medical imaging.
tips: Brush up on linear algebra and signals & systems first. Pair with EE 367.
description: Digital photography and basic image processing, convolutional neural networks for image processing, denoising, deconvolution, single pixel imaging, inverse problems in imaging, proximal gradient methods, introduction to wave optics, time-of-flight imaging, end-to-end optimization of optics and imaging processing. Emphasis is on applied image processing and solving inverse problems using classic algorithms, formal optimization, and modern artificial intelligence techniques. Students learn to apply material by implementing and investigating image processing algorithms in Python. Term project.
note: Offered in Winter 2026–27; no stable course-site link found.

title: Introduction to Robotics (ME 320)
one: Robotics fundamentals: kinematics, statics, dynamics, planning, and control.
pos: CS 223A (ME 320) is taught by Oussama Khatib and is the classic introduction to robotics. It covers spatial transformations, forward/inverse kinematics, Jacobians and statics, dynamics, trajectory planning, and classical control, with demos on physical robot platforms/simulation.
topics: **Spatial transformations**: rotation matrices, homogeneous transforms, quaternions
**Jacobians and statics**: velocity mapping, force transmission
**Trajectories and planning**: interpolation, obstacle avoidance, RRT
prereq: Matrix algebra; programming basics.
assessment: Assignments plus a project/exam. Check the current syllabus for details.
who: Robotics beginners; people interested in manipulation, control, or embodied AI; ME/EE/CS backgrounds all fit.
tips: Brush up on linear algebra and rigid-body transforms first. Pair with CS 225A for hands-on work.
description: Robotics foundations in modeling, design, planning, and control. Class covers relevant results from geometry, kinematics, statics, dynamics, motion planning, and control, providing the basic methodologies and tools in robotics research and applications. Concepts and models are illustrated through physical robot platforms, interactive robot simulations, and video segments relevant to historical research developments or to emerging application areas in the field. Recommended: matrix algebra.
note: Offered in Winter 2026–27; the official site is unavailable, so only the ExploreCourses link is provided.

zh: 机器人自主性原理 I
title: Principles of Robot Autonomy I (AA 274A, EE 260A, ME 274A)
one: Autonomous robots I: perception, localization, SLAM, nonlinear control, motion planning, and POMDPs.
pos: CS 237A (AA 274A/EE 260A/ME 274A) is taught by Marco Pavone and is the core course on robot autonomy. It connects perception, localization, control, planning, and decision-making under uncertainty, with extensive hands-on ROS work.
topics: **Localization and SLAM**: EKF, particle filters, graph optimization
**Motion planning**: graph search, sampling-based planning, trajectory optimization
**Project**: make a robot complete a task autonomously
prereq: CS 106A; CME 100 (linear algebra); CME 106 (probability).
assessment: Assignments plus a ROS project. Check the current syllabus for details.
who: Robotics, autonomous driving, drones, and embodied AI.
tips: Take CS 223A first or have rigid-body kinematics basics. Get familiar with ROS early.
description: Basic principles for endowing mobile autonomous robots with perception, planning, and decision-making capabilities. Algorithmic approaches for robot perception, localization, and simultaneous localization and mapping; control of non-linear systems, learning-based control, and robot motion planning; introduction to methodologies for reasoning under uncertainty, e.g., (partially observable) Markov decision processes. Extensive use of the Robot Operating System (ROS) for demonstrations and hands-on activities. Prerequisites: CS 106A or equivalent, CME 100 or equivalent (for linear algebra), and CME 106 or equivalent (for probability theory).

zh: 机器人自主性原理 II
title: Principles of Robot Autonomy II (AA 174B, AA 274B, EE 260B, ME 274B)
one: Autonomous robots II: RL/optimal control, manipulation, imitation learning, human-robot interaction, and system architecture.
pos: CS 237B is the advanced follow-up to CS 237A, shifting from mobility to learning new skills and physical interaction. It covers RL and optimal control, contact dynamics, grasping/manipulation, imitation learning, human intent inference, and system architecture validation, implemented on a mobile manipulation platform.
topics: **RL and optimal control**: MDPs, LQR, policy gradients
**Contact and manipulation**: grasping, non-prehensile manipulation, force control
**Imitation learning**: behavior cloning, DAgger, inverse RL
assessment: Assignments plus a project on a mobile manipulation platform. Check the current syllabus for details.
who: Robot manipulation, embodied AI, and human-robot collaboration.
tips: Take CS 237A and CS 234 first. Pair contact dynamics with physics simulation.
description: This course teaches advanced principles for endowing mobile autonomous robots with capabilities to autonomously learn new skills and to physically interact with the environment and with humans. It also provides an overview of different robot system architectures. Concepts that will be covered in the course are: Reinforcement Learning and its relationship to optimal control, contact and dynamics models for prehensile and non-prehensile robot manipulation, imitation learning and human intent inference, as well as different system architectures and their verification. Students will earn the theoretical foundations for these concepts and implement them on mobile manipulation platforms. In homeworks, the Robot Operating System (ROS) will be used extensively for demonstrations and hands-on activities. Prerequisites: CS106A or equivalent, CME 100 or equivalent (for linear algebra), CME 106 or equivalent (for probability theory), and AA 171/274.
note: Not offered in the 2026–27 ExploreCourses listing.

title: Experimental Robotics
one: Experimental robotics: hands-on kinematics, dynamics, control, compliance, and collision avoidance for robot arms.
pos: CS 225A is Khatib's lab course, emphasizing making robots actually move. It covers robot-arm kinematics, dynamics, control, compliant control, sensor-based collision avoidance, and human interfaces; the second half is an open project.
topics: **Open project**: drawing, air hockey, table tennis, etc.
prereq: CS 223A or equivalent.
assessment: Labs/assignments plus a final project demo. Check the current syllabus for details.
