who: People who want hands-on robotics, manipulation, or control; undergraduates/master's students preparing for a robotics lab.
tips: Take CS 223A first. When forming teams, cover control, perception, and software.
description: Hands-on laboratory course experience in robotic manipulation. Topics include robot kinematics, dynamics, control, compliance, sensor-based collision avoidance, and human-robot interfaces. Second half of class is devoted to final projects using various robotic platforms to build and demonstrate new robot task capabilities. Previous projects include the development of autonomous robot behaviors of drawing, painting, playing air hocket, yoyo, basketball, ping-pong or xylophone. Prerequisites: 223A or equivalent.

title: Robot Perception (EE 227)
one: Robot perception: vision/tactile/acoustic sensors plus algorithms, building a vision-based robot system in simulation.
pos: CS 227A (EE 227) is taught by Shuran Song and focuses on how robots understand the environment from raw sensor data and make decisions. It covers sensor hardware, calibration, visual perception, state estimation, and decision-making; assignments build a vision-based robot system step by step.
prereq: Python programming; linear algebra; math basics are reviewed in class, but programming demands are high.
assessment: A series of programming assignments plus an optional final report (4 units). Check the current syllabus for details.
who: Robot perception, embodied AI, and 3D vision.
tips: Take CS 231N or CS 237A first. The assignments are programming-heavy; get comfortable with PyTorch and simulation.
description: Robot Perception is the cornerstone of modern robotics, enabling machines to interpret, understand, and respond to an array of sensory information they encounter. In the course, students will study the basic principles of typical sensor hardware on a robotics system (e.g., vision, tactile, and acoustic sensors), the algorithms that process the raw sensory data, and make actionable decisions from that information. Over the course of the semester, students will incrementally build their own vision-based robotics system in simulation via a series of homework coding assignments. Students enrolling 4 units will be required to submit an additional final written report. Prerequisites: This course requires programming experience in python as well as basic knowledge of linear algebra. Most of the required mathematical concepts will be reviewed, but it will be assumed that students have strong programming skills. All the homework requires extensive programming.
note: Offered in Autumn 2026–27; no stable course-site link found.

zh: 具身智能的感知运动学习
title: Sensorimotor Learning for Embodied Agents (EE 381)
one: Sensorimotor learning for embodied agents: from raw perception to decisions, continuously adapting to the physical world.
pos: CS 381 (EE 381) is Shuran Song's advanced course for graduate students who want to do research on large models + robotics. It discusses the difference between embodied AI and internet AI, learning from raw perception to decisions, and continuous adaptation through hardware/software, with an emphasis on paper reading, critical discussion, and projects.
topics: **Embodied AI**: definitions, differences from internet AI
prereq: Deep learning, robotics/RL basics; research-oriented.
assessment: Paper reading/presentation/debate plus a project. Check the current syllabus for details.
who: People who want to do embodied AI research, robot learning, or VLA; students preparing for a PhD.
tips: Take CS 227A/CS 237B/CS 234 first. The project needs a real robot or a high-fidelity simulation.
description: This is an advanced course that will focus on modern machine learning algorithms for autonomous robots as an embodied intelligent agent. It covers advanced topics that center around 1. what is embodied AI and how it differs from internet AI, 2. how embodied agents perceive their environment from raw sensory data and make decisions, and 3. continually adapt to the physical world through both hardware and software improvements. By the end of the course, we hope to prepare you for conducting research in this area, knowing how to formulate the problem, design the algorithm, critically validate the idea through experimental designs and finally clearly present and communicate the findings. Students are expected to read, present, and debate the latest research papers on embodied AI, as well as obtain hands-on experience through the course projects.
note: Offered in Winter 2026–27; no stable course-site link found.

zh: 基因组与生物医学中的深度学习
title: Deep Learning in Genomics and Biomedicine (BMDS 273, GENE 236)
one: Deep learning in genomics and biomedicine: supervised, unsupervised, and generative models plus interpretability.
pos: Taught by James Zou, CS 273B is one of the most popular AI4Bio courses. It first covers deep learning and genomics background, then applies supervised, unsupervised, and generative models to biomedical data, emphasizing biological insights extracted from models, and ends with a team project on real data.
topics: **Supervised prediction**: disease risk, drug response, regulation
prereq: Calculus, linear algebra, probability/statistics (CS 109); machine learning (CS 229); no genomics background required.
assessment: Paper discussion plus a team project and assignments. Check the current syllabus for details.
who: Bioinformatics, computational biology, medical AI, and AI4Science; biology backgrounds moving into ML.
tips: Take CS 229 first. Pick a dataset with a clear biological question; don't just chase accuracy.
description: Recent breakthroughs in high-throughput genomic and biomedical data are transforming biological sciences into "big data" disciplines. In parallel, progress in deep neural networks are revolutionizing fields such as image recognition, natural language processing and, more broadly, AI. This course explores the exciting intersection between these two advances. The course will start with an introduction to deep learning and overview the relevant background in genomics and high-throughput biotechnology, focusing on the available data and their relevance. It will then cover the ongoing developments in deep learning (supervised, unsupervised and generative models) with the focus on the applications of these methods to biomedical data, which are beginning to produced dramatic results. In addition to predictive modeling, the course emphasizes how to visualize and extract interpretable, biological insights from such models. Recent papers from the literature will be presented and discussed. Experts in the field will present guest lectures. Students will be introduced to and work with popular deep learning software frameworks. Students will work in groups on a final class project using real world datasets. Prerequisites: College calculus, linear algebra, basic probability and statistics such as CS 109, and basic machine learning such as CS 229. No prior knowledge of genomics is necessary.
note: Offered in Spring 2026–27; no stable course-site link found.

title: Foundation Models for Healthcare (BMDS 271, RAD 271)
one: Foundation models for healthcare: training, evaluating, and deploying NLP/CV/multimodal FMs.
pos: CS 277 discusses how generative AI and self-supervised foundation models are changing healthcare. It covers NLP, CV, and multimodal models, both adapting general models to healthcare and building healthcare-specific FMs, with attention to evaluation, deployment, and real clinical needs.
topics: **Evaluation and deployment**: clinical metrics, regulation, bias
prereq: CS 229/231N/224N-level ML background.
assessment: Assignments plus a project/paper discussion. Check the current syllabus for details.
who: Medical AI, clinical data science, and medical imaging; engineers/researchers entering healthcare FMs.
tips: Take CS 231N or CS 224N first. Pay attention to privacy and regulatory constraints on clinical data.
description: Generative AI and large-scale self-supervised foundation models are poised to have a profound impact on human decision making across occupations. Healthcare is one such area where such models have the capacity to impact patients, clinicians, and other care providers. In this course, we will explore the training, evaluation, and deployment of generative AI and foundation models, with a focus on addressing current and future medical needs. The course will cover models used in natural language processing, computer vision, and multi-modal applications. We will explore the intersection of models trained on non-healthcare domains and their adaptation to domain-specific problems, as well as healthcare-specific foundation models. Prerequisites: Familiarity with machine learning principles at the level of CS 229, 231N, or 224N

zh: 计算生物学：生物分子与细胞的结构和组织
title: Computational Biology: Structure and Organization of Biomolecules and Cells (BIOE 279, BIOPHYS 279, BMDS 245, CME 279)
one: Computational biology: protein structure prediction/design, molecular simulation, drug screening, and microscopy image analysis.
pos: Taught by Ron Dror, CS 279 covers the three themes of structure, dynamics, and design in computational biology. It goes from protein structure prediction to protein design, drug screening, molecular dynamics, cell simulation, and microscopy image analysis — a core course for understanding AI4Bio in the AlphaFold era.
topics: **Protein structure prediction**: AlphaFold, Rosetta, homology modeling
**Drug screening**: docking, virtual screening, ML scoring
**Molecular simulation**: MD, free energy, enhanced sampling
prereq: CS 106A; introductory biology/biochemistry.
assessment: Assignments plus a project, possibly with paper discussion. Check the current syllabus for details.
who: Computational biology, drug discovery, and AI4Science; biology/chemistry backgrounds moving into computing.
tips: Brush up on molecular biology first. Pair with CS 273B for machine learning.
description: Computational techniques for investigating and designing the three-dimensional structure and dynamics of biomolecules and cells. These computational methods play an increasingly important role in drug discovery, medicine, bioengineering, and molecular biology. Course topics include protein structure prediction, protein design, drug screening, molecular simulation, cellular-level simulation, image analysis for microscopy, and methods for solving structures from crystallography and electron microscopy data. Prerequisites: elementary programming background (CS 106A or equivalent) and an introductory course in biology or biochemistry.

zh: 计算机视觉与生物医学进阶
title: Advanced Topics in Computer Vision and Biomedicine (BMDS 276)
one: Advanced CV + biomedicine: visual foundation models, diffusion/generation, and vision-language deployment in healthcare.
pos: Taught by Serena Yeung, CS 286 discusses visual foundation models in biomedicine in depth. It covers representation learning, diffusion/generative models, and vision-language models, as well as real deployment issues such as model size, compute, training/inference settings, and data.
topics: **Compute and data**: model scale, training/inference, data bias
prereq: CS 231N or BIODS 220-level deep learning/vision background.
assessment: Paper analysis plus class discussion and a final project. Check the current syllabus for details.
who: Graduate students in medical imaging, CV research, or AI4Science.
tips: Take CS 231N first. The course is research-oriented; pick a narrow clinical problem and go deep.
description: This course in artificial intelligence will provide a deep dive into advanced computer vision techniques for reasoning about visual data, and their real-world use in biomedicine. We will cover current cutting-edge models including different families of vision foundation models from representation learners to diffusion and generative models, and both vision-only and vision-language models. We will also cover considerations for real-world use, including model size and computation, training and inference settings, and training data, focusing on applications in biomedicine. Students will be actively engaged in studying and analyzing recent advancements through written analyses, class discussions, and a final project. This course is considered an advanced course and students should be comfortable with deep learning and computer vision at the level of CS231N or BIODS220.
note: Offered in Autumn 2026–27; no stable course-site link found.

title: Data Centric AI for Healthcare (BMDS 218)
one: Data-centric AI for healthcare: how data is generated, how bias/missingness/leakage break models, and how to fix it.
pos: Taught by Emily Alsentzer, Jason Fries, and others, CS 287 takes the opposite view from most ML courses: it studies data, not models. It discusses how clinical workflows, documentation habits, and institutional practices introduce bias, noise, missingness, and spurious correlations, and gives practical methods for data quality, labeling, synthetic data, and drift monitoring.
topics: **Data quality**: bias, noise, missingness, spurious correlations
prereq: Machine learning basics; interest in healthcare data.
assessment: Case discussion plus a project/assignment. Check the current syllabus for details.
who: Medical AI, clinical data science, and data engineering; anyone frustrated by 'the model is great but breaks in production'.
tips: It complements CS 277: 277 is models, 287 is data. Try to touch a real clinical data workflow for the project.
description: This course explores how healthcare data is generated in practice - and how these processes influence the development of robust, trustworthy machine learning models. Students will examine how clinical workflows, documentation habits, and institutional practices introduce bias, noise, missingness, and spurious correlations into datasets. The course emphasizes the often-overlooked reality that many model failures stem not from algorithmic design, but from subtle flaws in how data is collected, labeled, and interpreted. Through lectures, real-world case studies, and observation of clinical data workflows, students will develop practical tools for understanding and improving data quality and model reliability. Topics include assessing data quality, addressing missingness and label leakage, developing scalable and accurate annotation strategies, leveraging synthetic data, and monitoring data and models for drift over time. Students will also learn to evaluate how these data challenges impact model generalization and robustness.
note: Offered in Winter 2026–27; no stable course-site link found.

zh: 面向神经科学的大规模神经网络建模
title: Large-Scale Neural Network Modeling for Neuroscience (PSYCH 249)
one: Model the brain with large-scale neural networks: vision, audition, motor control, language, and decision-making as convergent evolution.
pos: Taught by Dan Yamins, CS 375 (PSYCH 249) is a core course at the intersection of computational neuroscience and AI. It discusses how the internal components of artificial networks correspond to real brain structure, covering feedforward perception, recurrent dynamics, attention/memory/navigation, language Transformers, self-supervision, and deep RL, and teaches how to quantitatively compare models with neural data.
topics: **Model-neural data comparison**: RSA, encoding models, metrics
prereq: Modern neural network background (one of CS 229/230/231N/234/236/330); no cognitive science/neuroscience background required.
assessment: Paper discussion plus a project. Check the current syllabus for details.
who: NeuroAI, computational neuroscience, and AI interpretability; people who want to use AI to understand the brain.
tips: Take CS 231N or CS 224N first. Pair with CS 322/EE 292R for a broader view.
description: The last ten years has seen a watershed in the development of large-scale neural networks in artificial intelligence. At the same time, computational neuroscientists have discovered a surprisingly robust mapping between the internal components of these networks and real neural structures in the human brain. In this class we will discuss a panoply of examples of such "convergent man-machine evolution", including: feedforward models of sensory systems (vision, audition, somatosensation); recurrent neural networks for dynamics and motor control; integrated models of attention, memory, and navigation; transformer models of language areas; self-supervised models of learning; and deep RL models of decision and planning. We will also delve into the methods and metrics for comparing such models to real-world neural data, and address how unsolved open problems in AI (that you can work on!) will drive forward novel neural models. Some meaningful background in modern neural networks is highly advised (e.g. CS229, CS230, CS231n, CS234, CS236, CS 330), but formal preparation in cognitive science or neuroscience is not needed (we will provide this).

zh: AI 与数据驱动的科学
title: AI and Data for Science (CS 292, PSYCH 292R, STATS 282)
one: AI4Science frontier lectures: one Stanford professor each week on how AI/data advances their scientific field.
pos: EE 292R (CS 292/PSYCH 292R/STATS 282) is a 1-unit seminar first offered in Autumn 2026, organized by Candès, Wetzstein, Narasimhan, and Wandell. It does not teach specific techniques; each week a speaker presents a real AI4Science case, covering neuroscience, medicine, genomics, computational social science, world models, and more.
topics: **Neuroscience**: retina/visual system, brain foundation models, digital twins
**Medicine**: medical imaging FMs, precision medicine, multimodal omics
**Spatial intelligence**: video world models, world agents
**Computational social science**: coordinated behavior detection across encrypted platforms
**Research infrastructure**: Marlowe GPU cluster, petabyte-scale data
prereq: No hard prerequisites; interest in AI + science is enough.
assessment: Attendance plus a short write-up on one lecture topic; 1 unit, S/NC.
who: People who want a fast map of AI4Science and to find interdisciplinary topics/collaborators; not for people who want systematic ML technique training.
tips: Lectures are in person only, but Stanford Online will upload recordings to YouTube. Write down one 'method + scientific question' pair per talk.
description: AI4Science is an emerging discipline that leverages machine learning, foundation models, and autonomous agents to accelerate the pace of discovery. By integrating data-driven architectures with physical constraints, the field models complex systems at unprecedented scales. At Stanford, this work is empowered by Marlowe - a specialized GPU-based computational instrument. This seminar series presents research from the Stanford community and beyond, exploring the frontier where Al and scientific inquiry converge.
instructors: Candes, E.; Wetzstein, G.; Narasimhan, B.; Wandell, B.

title: Human-Centered AI
one: Norvig's human-centered AI: user mental models, trustworthy design, fairness, and ethics.
pos: Taught by Peter Norvig, CS 139 discusses how AI systems are understood and used by people. It focuses on users' mental models of AI, how trust forms, explainability, fairness and justice, and AI's impact on the economy and daily life; it is not a model-training course but a course on making AI useful and acceptable to people.
topics: **User models**: how people understand AI, how expectations form
**Fairness and justice**: bias, distributive justice, procedural justice
**Economic and social impact**: jobs, power, the information ecosystem
**Ethical frameworks**: respect for persons, beneficence, fairness
prereq: No strong technical prerequisites; interest in AI products/policy/ethics.
assessment: Reading/discussion plus a paper/project. Check the current syllabus for details.
who: Product managers, designers, and policy/law backgrounds; technical people who want the human dimension.
tips: Pair with CS 281 for technical fairness/interpretability and CS 247A for design practice.
description: Artificial Intelligence technology can and must be guided by human concerns. The course examines how mental models and user models of AI systems are formed, and how that leads to user expectations. This informs a set of design guidelines for building AI systems that are trustworthy, understandable, fair, and beneficial. The course covers the impact of AI systems on the economy and everyday life, and ethical issues of collecting data and running systems, including respect for persons, beneficence, fairness and justice.
note: Offered in Winter 2026–27; no stable course-site link found.

title: Design for Artificial Intelligence (SYMSYS 195A)
one: Design for human-centered AI: a studio course of research, prototyping, and iteration toward responsible AI experiences.
pos: CS 247A (SYMSYS 195A) is the advanced design follow-up to CS 147, run entirely as a studio. It focuses on human-centered AI experiences: what AI is, what constraints and opportunities it has, and how to design responsible, ethical AI systems. The course emphasizes intense iteration and real design problems.
topics: **AI capabilities and constraints**: what it can and cannot do
**Trust and transparency**: explanations, control, error recovery
prereq: CS 147 or equivalent design-thinking background; application may be required.
assessment: Studio attendance plus iteration and a final project. Check the current syllabus for details.
who: Designers, product managers, HCI students; AI developers moving from demos to experiences.
tips: This is not an ML technique course. Confirm you can commit studio time before enrolling.
description: A project-based course that builds on the introduction to design in CS147 by focusing on advanced methods and tools for research, prototyping, and user interface design. Studio based format with intensive coaching and iteration to prepare students for tackling real world design problems. This course takes place entirely in studios; you must plan on attending every studio to take this class. The focus of CS247A is design for human-centered artificial intelligence experiences. What does it mean to design for AI? What is HAI? How do you create responsible, ethical, human centered experiences? Let us explore what AI actually is and the constraints, opportunities and specialized processes necessary to create AI systems that work effectively for the humans involved. Prerequisites: CS147 or equivalent background in design thinking. In the event of a waitlist, acceptance to class based on an application provided on the first day of class.
note: Not offered in the 2026–27 ExploreCourses listing.

title: Ethics of Artificial Intelligence
one: The technical side of AI ethics: fairness, interpretability, privacy, and the formal limits of these methods.
pos: CS 281 is not pure philosophical discussion; it uses ML methods to address fairness, bias, transparency, and privacy. The course identifies unfair or untruthful problems through cases, applies detection and mitigation techniques, and discusses the formal limits and real trade-offs of these techniques.
topics: **Bias detection**: data bias, model bias, auditing
prereq: CS 229 or equivalent ML background.
assessment: Assignments plus a project/paper. Check the current syllabus for details.
who: People who want responsible AI, AI auditing, or policy technology; anyone who wants a hands-on ethics course.
tips: Pair with CS 139 for the human perspective and CS 221M for model internals.
description: Machine learning has become an indispensable tool for creating intelligent applications, accelerating scientific discoveries, and making better data-driven decisions. Yet, the automation and scaling of such tasks can have troubling negative societal impacts. Through practical case studies, you will identify issues of fairness, justice and truth in AI applications. You will then apply recent techniques to detect and mitigate such algorithmic biases, along with methods to provide more transparency and explainability to state-of-the-art ML models. Finally, you will derive fundamental formal results on the limits of such techniques, along with tradeoffs that must be made for their practical application. CS229 or equivalent classes or experience.
note: Not offered in the 2026–27 ExploreCourses listing.

zh: 构建与评估 AI 产品
title: Building and Evaluating AI Products
one: Build an AI product and agent from 0 to 1: AI fit, latency/quality/cost, evaluation, and Demo Day.
pos: MS&E 203 is a project-based course where students build a real AI product in one quarter. It requires justifying why AI is needed, handling latency/quality/cost trade-offs, rigorously evaluating the system, and presenting at Demo Day. Before enrolling, students complete self-study modules on git, AI coding tools, eval frameworks, and APIs.
topics: **Team build**: from individual mechanisms to a team product
prereq: Upper-level undergraduates/master's students; programming ability; capacity about 48 students (12 teams × 4).
assessment: Mainly a project plus Demo Day; individual/team assignments may be included. Check the current syllabus for details.
who: People who want to start a company or build AI products; MS&E, CS, SymSys, EE backgrounds; anyone who needs a portfolio.
tips: Build a complementary team (engineering + design + business). Don't pick too large a problem; evaluation matters more than the demo.
description: A project-based course on building AI products and agents end-to-end. Students build a real product over the quarter, justifying AI fit, navigating latency, quality, and cost trade-offs, and rigorously evaluating their own system. The course moves from an individual mechanics phase into a team build, ending in a Demo Day. Enrolled students complete a self-paced pre-course module covering git basics, AI coding tool fluency (Cursor, Claude Code, or Antigravity), eval framework basics, and API setup. Designed primarily for upper-division undergraduates and master's students, with target majors including MS&E, CS, Symbolic Systems, and EE; open to all Stanford students. Enrollment is capped at 12 teams of 4 students (48 students total).
instructors: Nahass, P.; Emrani, D.; Udell, M.

title: Statistical Learning and Data Science
one: An introduction to statistical learning: regression/classification, regularization, trees/ensembles, SVMs, neural networks, and clustering.
pos: STATS 202 is the core data-science course in the statistics department, taught by Robert Tibshirani and others. It covers the main supervised and unsupervised methods from a statistical perspective, emphasizing model selection, evaluation, and interpretability. It is more applied and inference-oriented than CS 229, and suits people interested in data science.
topics: **Nonlinear methods**: splines, GAMs, trees, random forests, boosting
**Neural networks and Transformers**: basics and applications
prereq: Probability/statistics and linear algebra; programming (R/Python).
assessment: Assignments plus an exam/project. Check the current syllabus for details.
who: Data science, statistical analysis, and business analytics; ML learners who want a statistical perspective.
tips: It complements CS 229: 202 emphasizes model evaluation and statistical inference, 229 emphasizes algorithm derivations.
description: Overview of supervised learning, with a focus on regression and classification methods. Syllabus includes: linear and polynomial regression, logistic regression and linear discriminant analysis; cross-validation and the bootstrap, model selection and regularization methods (ridge and lasso); nonlinear models, splines and generalized additive models; tree-based methods, random forests and boosting; support-vector machines; Neural nets and transformers; Some unsupervised learning: principal components and clustering (k-means and hierarchical).

title: Modern Applied Statistics: Learning
one: Modern applied statistical learning: prediction methods, model evaluation, optimization, and generative models.
pos: STATS 315A is a graduate-level ML course in the statistics department, covering prediction methods (linear models, trees/forests, deep networks), model evaluation (cross-validation, calibration, conformal prediction), optimization (convexity, stochastic methods), and generative models (language models, diffusion, VAEs). It balances statistical rigor with modern methods.
prereq: Probability/statistics, linear algebra, ML basics (STATS 202/CS 229 level).
assessment: Assignments plus a project/exam. Check the current syllabus for details.
who: Statistics/ML graduate students; people who want rigorous predictive modeling and uncertainty quantification.
tips: Take STATS 202 or CS 229 first. The conformal prediction part is worth going deep on.
description: This course covers statistical techniques underlying modern machine learning. Topics include prediction methods (linear models, trees and forests, deep neural networks), model evaluation (cross-validation, calibration, conformal prediction), optimization (convexity, stochastic methods, adaptive metrics), and generative models (language models, diffusion models, variational autoencoders).

title: Safe and Constrained AI

Each week highlights a key theoretical result alongside state-of-the-art research, with applications spanning robotics, finance, healthcare, energy, and language models. description: Machine learning and data analysis have enjoyed tremendous success in a broad range of domains. These advances hold the promise of great benefits to individuals, organizations and society. Undeniably, algorithms are informing decisions that reach ever more deeply into our lives, from news article recommendations to criminal sentencing decisions to healthcare diagnostics. This progress, however, raises (and is impeded by) a host of concerns regarding the societal impact of computation. A prominent concern is that these algorithms should be fair. Unfortunately, the hope that automated decision-making might be free of social biases is dashed on the data on which the algorithms are trained and the choices in their construction: left to their own devices, algorithms will propagate - even amplify - existing biases of the data, the programmers, and the decisions made in the choice of features to incorporate and measurements of 'fitness' to be applied. Addressing wrongful discrimination by algorithms is not only mandated by law and by ethics but is essential to maintaining the public trust in the current computation-driven revolution.The study of fairness is ancient and multi-disciplinary: philosophers, legal experts, economists, statisticians, social scientists and others have been concerned with fairness for as long as these fields have existed. Nevertheless, the scale of decision making in the age of big-data, the computational complexities of algorithmic decision making, and simple professional responsibility mandate that computer scientists contribute to this research endeavor. This is an intro to this booming area of research. Prerequisites: CS 161. I will be assuming some mathematical maturity, CS 154 is recommended.

description: Artificial Intelligence (AI) measurement science provides frameworks and methodologies for evaluating, benchmarking, and understanding AI systems. As AI systems become increasingly powerful and deploy into high-stakes domains, the need for rigorous measurement approaches has grown in importance. Current measurement approaches are often ad hoc, lacking theoretical grounding, and failing to connect to real-world use cases. This has led to a measurement crisis characterized by benchmark saturation, inconsistent evaluation methodologies, and difficulty in making valid claims about AI capabilities. This course will cover the foundations of AI measurement science from first principles and outline connections to the growing literature on the topic. This includes: validity theory as applied to AI evaluation, focusing on content, criterion, construct, external, and consequential validity; psychometric models for AI measurement, including item response theory and latent variable models; scaling laws and intervention effects, predicting the impacts of data, computing, and architecture choices; synthetic data generation for evaluation and its implications; governance and policy considerations around AI measurement. This is a graduate-level course. By the end of the course, students should be able to understand, implement, and critique state-of-the-art AI measurement approaches and be ready to conduct research on these topics.

As large-scale textual data continues to grow, statistical methods are crucial for detecting patterns, analyzing linguistic trends, and constructing efficient, interpretable models. Key topics include: Word Frequency Distributions (Zipf's and Heaps' laws); Entropy & Information Theory (redundancy and uncertainty in language); Probabilistic Language Models (n-grams, smoothing, perplexity); Markov Models & Hidden Markov Chains (stochastic text sequences); Text Similarity & Distance Metrics (measuring divergence in text); Corpus Statistics & Sampling (estimating linguistic trends); Random Processes in Text Generation (stochastic models of language). By the end of the course, students will develop a strong foundation in statistical text analysis, equipping them with essential tools for computational linguistics, AI, search technologies, and digital humanities in an increasingly data-driven world.

This lecture course offers a non-technical exploration of its foundational principles, inherent strengths and limitations, and a comprehensive overview of its profound impact on our society and economy. We will delve into critical questions: How will AI reshape labor markets and jobs? What roles will it play in medical research, healthcare, education, entertainment, engineering, transportation, and the legal system? How will it be used - or misused - in democratic societies and autocratic regimes? Will it alter the geopolitical balance of power and the nature of warfare? How can we align these powerful systems with human values? Can machines genuinely create, or possess consciousness? Does the prospect of superintelligence mean the human race is doomed? Will the benefits of this technological revolution be broadly distributed, or accrue to a lucky few? Are we currently experiencing an 'AI bubble'? This course also demystifies essential jargon, such as 'transformers', 'prompt engineering', 'chain of thought', 'hallucination', 'jailbreaking', 'context rot', 'deepfakes', 'stochastic parrots', and 'algorithmic bias'. By equipping students with historical grounding, intellectual tools, ethical frameworks, and psychological perspectives, this course prepares them to thoughtfully navigate the complexities of the AI revolution.
